data_section_full_text:
3. Data


EDGAR server log overview

The EDGAR database provides investors with online access to all mandated SEC filings
since 1996. The SEC maintains server logs that record every request for a public filing on
EDGAR via its website. These logs are not publicly available but were privately provided
to us by the SEC for research purposes. The server log data we employ includes all
requests from all users for the 4-year period from January 1, 2008 to December 31, 2011.
Each log entry provides the following information:

1. The IP address of the requesting user, with the final octet of the address replaced
with a unique set of three letters. <sup>8</sup>

2. The date and time of the request.
3. The CIK (Central Index Key) of the company that filed the requested form.
4. A link to the particular filing, which includes the form’s accession number that
uniquely identifies a particular filing.


To identify particular companies, we match the CIK in the EDGAR server log to that in
COMPUSTAT. To identify a particular filing, we download the Master Index File for all
available time periods from the SEC website. <sup>9</sup> The Master Index provides accession numbers (the unique identifier of a given filing), filing dates, and the filing name (e.g., “8-K”)
for each filing, which we match to a given accession number from our ESV data set.

The ESV database offers several other advantageous features. Perhaps most importantly, it reflects the activity of users, where the IP address is the proxy for an individual
user. This database reveals the activities of nearly 10 million unique users—such a largescale view of information acquisition is virtually nonexistent in the literature. <sup>10</sup> Second, it

8. The SEC replaced the final octet with letters to preserve the privacy of the user. For example, a hypothetical IP address in the database would appear as “001.232.064.agx.”
9. The EDGAR Master Index File is available at [ftp://ftp.sec.gov/edgar/full-index.](http://https://www.sec.gov/info/edgar/forms/edgform.pdf) We thank Andy Leone for
providing the PERL program used to download the index (see [http://sbaleone.bus.miami.edu/PERL-](http://edgar.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/789019/000119312512316848/0001193125-12-316848-index.htm)
[COURSE/Perl_Resources.html).](http://edgar.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/789019/000119312512316848/0001193125-12-316848-index.htm)
10. For the remainder of the paper, we use the term “information acquisition” to refer to EDGAR users
retrieving documents from the EDGAR system.

Third, it reflects a user’s decision to access a specific piece of information from the
myriad of readily available financial disclosures. Thus, our data allow us to observe variation in the timing, choices, and magnitude of information access. Finally, the data come
directly from the primary source of regulatory disclosure—the SEC. Other research examining information demand uses indirect proxies for the acquired information, such as
search engine logs (e.g., Drake et al. 2012) or information from data aggregators, which is
often delayed or inaccurate relative to the SEC filing time and date. <sup>11</sup> In summary, these
